# 1 Samuel Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 167v–168r | **Source Image:** 1SA_013_page_001.jpg, 1SA_013_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Saul was [thirty] years old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel for [forty-]two years.

**2** Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the forces he sent home.

**3** Jonathan struck down the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. Then Saul had the trumpet blown throughout the land, declaring, "Let the Hebrews hear!"

**4** All Israel heard the news: "Saul has attacked the Philistine garrison, and now Israel has become an offense to the Philistines!" So the people were summoned to join Saul at Gilgal.

**5** The Philistines assembled to fight Israel — three thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and foot soldiers as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They came up and encamped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.

**6** When the men of Israel saw that they were in a desperate situation — for the army was hard-pressed — the people hid in caves, thickets, among rocks, in pits, and in cisterns.

**7** Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan into the territory of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and the entire army with him was trembling with fear.

**8** He waited seven days, the time Samuel had set. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to scatter.

**9** So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the fellowship offerings." And he offered the burnt offering himself.

**10** Just as he finished presenting the burnt offering, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to greet him.

**11** Samuel demanded, "What have you done?" Saul replied, "When I saw that the troops were scattering, and you had not come within the appointed days, and the Philistines were massing at Michmash —

**12** I thought, 'The Philistines are about to come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the LORD's favor.' So I felt compelled to offer the burnt offering myself."

**13** Samuel said to Saul, "You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the command the LORD your God gave you. If you had, the LORD would have established your dynasty over Israel permanently.

**14** But now your dynasty will not endure. The LORD has already sought out a man after his own heart and appointed him as ruler over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."

**15** Then Samuel set out from Gilgal and went up to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counted the troops who remained with him — about six hundred men.

**16** Saul and his son Jonathan, along with the soldiers who were with them, were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines were encamped at Michmash.

**17** Raiding parties went out from the Philistine camp in three detachments. One turned toward Ophrah in the region of Shual,

**18** another turned toward Beth-horon, and the third turned toward the border that overlooks the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.

**19** Now there was not a single blacksmith to be found in all the land of Israel, because the Philistines had said, "The Hebrews must not be allowed to make swords or spears."

**20** So every Israelite had to go down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle.

**21** The charge was two-thirds of a shekel for plowshares and mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening axes and setting ox-goads.

**22** So on the day of battle, not a single sword or spear could be found among any of the troops with Saul and Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.

**23** Meanwhile, a Philistine outpost had advanced to the pass of Michmash.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — The corrupted regnal formula:** The Hebrew text here is one of the most famous textual difficulties in the Bible. The Leningrad Codex reads בֶּן־שָׁנָה שָׁאוּל בְּמָלְכוֹ — literally "Saul was a son of a year when he became king" — which is obviously impossible. The number has been lost from the manuscript tradition. The brackets in the translation indicate scholarly reconstruction; "thirty" and "forty-two" are conventional supplements, but the original numbers are simply not recoverable from any Hebrew witness. The formula itself mirrors the standard regnal formula used for all kings of Israel and Judah (cf. 2 Samuel 5:4, 1 Kings 14:21).

**Verse 8 — "the time Samuel had set":** This refers back to Samuel's instruction in 10:8. The seven-day wait is a test of obedience, not merely a scheduling matter. Saul's failure is not impatience in the ordinary sense — it is a failure to trust that God's prophet speaks with God's authority and God's timing.

**Verses 9–12 — Saul's unlawful sacrifice:** Saul's self-justification is a masterpiece of narrative psychology. He presents a chain of reasonable excuses: the troops were deserting, Samuel was late, the enemy was advancing. Each excuse is factually true. But the issue is not the circumstances — it is who has the authority to offer sacrifice. By usurping the priestly/prophetic function, Saul reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of his role: the king serves under God's word through the prophet, not above it.

**Verse 14 — "a man after his own heart":** The Hebrew אִישׁ כִּלְבָבוֹ is the first veiled reference to David in the narrative. The phrase does not mean a man who perfectly mirrors God's emotions, but rather a man whom God has chosen according to his own purpose — a man of God's own seeking. The contrast with Saul is not moral perfection versus moral failure, but responsiveness to divine authority versus self-reliant pragmatism.

**Verses 19–22 — The Philistine iron monopoly:** This remarkable aside reveals the depth of Israel's subjugation. The Philistines controlled iron-working technology (they were among the Sea Peoples who brought iron-age metallurgy to Canaan). By banning blacksmiths, they ensured permanent military dominance. Israel's army was essentially disarmed — fighting with farm tools against iron weapons. This technological detail makes Jonathan's single-handed raid in chapter 14 all the more astonishing, and underscores that Israel's victories come from God, not superior arms.

— PNEUMA
